money-growth-inflation-s1.title: Money, velocity and real GDP in Ostra (invented)

table.caption: Ostra, an invented country: money supply, velocity and real GDP

money-growth-inflation-s2.title: Fast money growth in Kaldo (invented country)
money-growth-inflation-s2.text: Kaldo, an invented country, pays many of its government's bills by having its central bank create new money. For several years the money supply has grown 40 percent a year. Velocity has stayed about the same, and real GDP has grown about 2 percent a year, in line with Kaldo's resources and technology.

items.q: Use $M \times V = P \times Y$. What is Ostra's nominal GDP in Year 1, in billions of dollars?

why.correct: Nominal GDP is $P \times Y = M \times V = 500 \times 4 = 2{,}000$ billion dollars.

mistakes.why: You divided the money supply by velocity. Nominal GDP is the money supply times the number of times each dollar is spent: 500 x 4.

items.q: What is Ostra's price level in Year 2? Give it as a number, where 1.0 means the base-year price level.

mistakes.why: You turned the formula upside down. Solve $M \times V = P \times Y$ for P: P = (M x V) / Y = 2,200 / 2,000.
That is nominal GDP (M x V). Divide it by real GDP to get the price level.

items.q: By what percent did Ostra's price level rise from Year 1 to Year 2?

why.correct: The Year 1 price level is $\frac{500 \times 4}{2{,}000} = 1.0$ and the Year 2 level is 1.1, so prices rose $\frac{1.1 - 1.0}{1.0} \times 100 = 10$ percent.

mistakes.why: That is the Year 2 price level itself. The inflation rate is its percent change from Year 1, (1.1 - 1.0) / 1.0 x 100.
That is the change in the money supply in billions of dollars. Find the percent change in the price level.

items.q: In the table, the money supply grows 10 percent while velocity and real GDP stay the same. Which statement fits the quantity theory?
options: Real GDP rises 10 percent, and the price level is unchanged
The price level rises by the same 10 percent, and real output is unchanged
Velocity falls 10 percent, so nothing else changes
The price level falls 10 percent, since each dollar can now buy more output

why.correct: If $V$ and $Y$ are fixed, $M \times V = P \times Y$ means $P$ moves in proportion to $M$.
options: The table shows real GDP unchanged; with V fixed, the extra money shows up in P.
Right: with V and Y fixed, P must rise in proportion to M so that both sides of the equation stay equal.
The table holds velocity at 4 in both years.
More money chasing the same output raises prices; each dollar buys less.

items.q: Use the growth-rate form of the quantity theory, inflation = money growth + velocity growth - real output growth. About what inflation rate should Kaldo expect?

why.correct: Velocity growth is about 0, so inflation $\approx 40 + 0 - 2 = 38$ percent a year.

mistakes.why: You added real output growth. More output soaks up some of the new money, so subtract it: 40 + 0 - 2.
That is the money growth rate. Real output also grew 2 percent, which uses some of the new money: 40 - 2.

items.q: In the long run, how does Kaldo's fast money growth affect its real GDP?
options: Little or no lasting effect: real output depends on resources and technology
It raises real GDP by about 40 percent a year
It lowers real GDP by about 38 percent a year
It raises real GDP by the amount of the new money divided by velocity

why.correct: Long-run neutrality of money: money growth changes nominal variables, not real output or the natural rate of unemployment.
options: Right: in the long run money is neutral; it changes prices and other nominal values, not how much the economy can produce.
Real GDP is growing about 2 percent, in line with resources and technology; the rest of the money growth becomes inflation.
The quantity theory says the extra money raises the price level; it does not shrink real output by that amount.
That treats new money as new production. Output is set by the economy's productive capacity.

items.q: Lenders in Kaldo come to expect this high inflation. What happens to the nominal interest rates they charge on new loans?
options: They fall, because there is more money available to lend
They stay the same, because the real interest rate is unchanged
They rise, because lenders add expected inflation to the real return they want
They fall to zero, because money loses value too quickly to lend

why.correct: Nominal rate = real rate + expected inflation. Expected inflation shows up in nominal interest rates.
options: More money does not lower nominal rates for long when lenders expect prices to rise fast; they need compensation for it.
An unchanged real rate means the nominal rate rises one for one with expected inflation.
Right: the nominal rate is roughly the real rate plus expected inflation, so higher expected inflation means higher nominal rates.
Lenders keep lending but demand a higher nominal rate to cover inflation.

items.q: Suppose Kaldo slows money growth to 2 percent a year, with velocity steady and real GDP still growing 2 percent. About what inflation rate follows in the long run?
options: About 2 percent
About 4 percent
About 38 percent
About 0 percent

why.correct: Inflation $\approx$ money growth + velocity growth - real output growth $= 2 + 0 - 2 = 0$.
options: That is the money growth rate alone; real output growth uses all of it.
You added output growth instead of subtracting it.
That was the inflation rate with 40 percent money growth.
Right: 2 + 0 - 2 is about 0. Money growth matches output growth, so the price level stays about the same.

items.q: A country's nominal GDP is 16 trillion dollars and its money supply is 2 trillion dollars. What is the velocity of money?

why.correct: $V = \frac{P \times Y}{M} = \frac{16}{2} = 8$: each dollar is spent on final goods and services about 8 times a year.

mistakes.why: You divided money by nominal GDP. Velocity is nominal GDP divided by the money supply: 16 / 2.

items.q: What does the velocity of money measure?
options: How many times a year the average dollar is spent on final goods and services
How fast the central bank adds new money to the economy
How quickly prices rise over a year
How many times a new deposit is lent and re-lent through the whole banking system

why.correct: From $M \times V = P \times Y$: $V = \frac{P \times Y}{M}$, nominal GDP per dollar of money.
options: Right: velocity is nominal GDP divided by the money supply.
That is the money growth rate, M changing, not V.
That is the inflation rate.
That describes the money multiplier process, not velocity.

items.q: An economy starts at full employment. The central bank increases the money supply once, and over time nominal wages adjust. Shift both curves that move and mark the new long-run equilibrium.

why.correct: More money lowers interest rates and raises spending, so AD shifts right. Output above full employment pushes nominal wages up, so SRAS shifts left. The economy ends at full-employment output with a higher price level.

key.because: more money (AD) and then higher nominal wages (SRAS)

slips.LRAS: Money does not change the economy's resources or technology, so LRAS stays at full-employment output.

items.q: A central bank permanently raises the money supply. Which of these changes in the long run?
options: Real GDP
The natural rate of unemployment
The real interest rate
The price level

why.correct: The long-run neutrality of money: money changes nominal variables, not real ones.
options: Real GDP returns to full-employment output, which depends on resources and technology.
The natural rate depends on frictional and structural unemployment, not on the amount of money.
In the long run the real interest rate is set by saving and investment, not by the money supply.
Right: in the long run the extra money raises the price level and other nominal values.

items.q: Why can a rise in the money supply raise real GDP in the short run but not in the long run?
options: Velocity doubles in the short run and then falls to zero
Nominal wages and some prices adjust slowly, so output can rise until they catch up
The central bank takes the money back out in the long run
LRAS shifts right in the short run and back left in the long run

why.correct: In the short run money is not neutral because of sticky wages and prices; in the long run it is.
options: The quantity theory treats velocity as roughly steady; it does not swing like this.
Right: sticky wages let a rise in AD raise output in the short run; once wages adjust, SRAS shifts left and output returns to full employment.
The money supply stays higher; it is the wage adjustment that removes the output gain.
LRAS depends on resources and technology, not on the money supply.

items.q: The money supply grows faster than real output for many years. Select every variable that ends up higher because of it.
options: The price level
Nominal GDP
Real GDP
The unemployment rate

why.correct: Money growth shows up in nominal variables (prices, nominal GDP, nominal wages), not in real output or unemployment, in the long run.
options: Right: faster money growth means a faster rise in the price level.
Right: nominal GDP equals M x V, which rises with M.
Real GDP depends on resources and technology; money is neutral in the long run.
Unemployment returns to the natural rate in the long run.

items.q: Velocity rises because people start paying with cards and spend money faster. If the money supply and real GDP stay the same, what happens to the price level?
options: It rises, because M x V is now larger while Y is unchanged
It falls, because money is spent faster and so is worth more
It stays the same, because the money supply did not change
It rises by exactly the rise in the money supply

why.correct: Both M and V feed nominal spending: with Y fixed, a rise in either raises the price level.
options: Right: P = (M x V) / Y, so a larger V raises P.
Faster spending of the same money raises nominal spending, which raises prices.
The price level depends on M x V, not on M alone.
The money supply did not change; the rise comes from velocity.

items.q: Build the long-run chain from fast money growth to inflation.

why.correct: Faster money growth raises nominal spending; with velocity steady and real output fixed by resources, the price level rises, so inflation rises.

specific.frame: The money supply grows faster, so nominal spending (M x V) ___. Velocity is steady and real output is set by ___, so the ___ rises, and ___ is unchanged in the long run.
specific.model: The money supply grows faster, so nominal spending (M x V) rises. Because velocity is steady and real output is set by resources and technology, the price level rises, which means higher inflation, and real GDP is unchanged in the long run.

spending.label: Nominal spending
options: rises
falls

why.1: More money times the same velocity is more spending, not less.

because.label: What sets real output
options: resources and technology
the money supply

why.1: In the long run output depends on productive capacity; that is what money neutrality means.

price.label: What rises
options: price level
velocity of money

why.1: Velocity is assumed steady; the price level absorbs the extra money.

output.label: What is unchanged
options: real GDP
nominal GDP

why.1: Nominal GDP equals M x V, so it rises with the money supply.
